My husband stopped snoring on a Tuesday. I know, because I was awake for all of it, waiting for the sound the way you wait for a dripping tap.

For years the routine was: elbow, roll over, five quiet minutes, start again. I'd moved to the spare room twice that month.

The strips didn't fix it. The spray definitely didn't.

What changed was his pillow, of all things. A contoured one that keeps his head and neck lined up instead of tipped back — because when the head tips, the airway narrows, and that's the noise.

Tuesday night: silence. I actually checked he was breathing.

It's been weeks now. He says his neck feels better. I just care that the bedroom is quiet and I'm sleeping in it.

If you — or the person next to you — rattles the windows at 2am, look at what the pillow is doing to their posture first. 👇

At 58 I assumed waking up with a stiff neck was just part of getting older.

Every morning started the same. Sit up slowly. Wince. Rub the right side of my neck through the first coffee.

I'd tried the expensive memory foam one. Flat in a month. I'd tried sleeping on two pillows. Worse.

Then my physio-obsessed daughter said something I couldn't unhear: "You spend eight hours a night with your head at an angle you'd never hold awake."

The fix wasn't stretches. It was a pillow shaped to hold my neck level — a butterfly contour with support wings, so my head sits in line instead of sinking.

The first night felt strange, like it was doing the holding for me. By the end of the week I was waking before the alarm with a loose neck and no headache.

I'm not saying it's magic. I'm saying my old pillow was the problem, and I'd spent two years blaming my age.

If your mornings start with a wince, it's worth seeing how the shape works. 👇

I did it three times. Each one arrived plump, lasted a few weeks, then packed down into the same shapeless slab. And every morning my neck paid for it.

What I ended up with isn't a softer pillow or a bigger one. It's a shaped one — a butterfly contour in high-density foam that decides the position for you. Neck level. Shoulders relaxed. Arms with somewhere to go.

And it doesn't pack flat, because the shape is the whole point.

I stopped waking up more tired than I went to bed. That's the entire review.

If you've bought three pillows in two years: stop replacing, start supporting. See how the shape works. 👇

ad_creative_bodies:
💔 There is a kind of homesickness that has nothing to do with a place.

It is being homesick for a person you love. A person you would give anything to see again, hear again, sit beside again.

After her husband died, a friend once told me that was the closest word she could find for what she felt.

Homesick.

She missed the sound of him walking through the house. The way he would say her name. The ordinary conversations that never seemed important until there were no more of them.

She missed having someone to tell the little things to.

She missed looking across the room and knowing he was there.

She even missed the things that used to drive her crazy. Funny how grief can make you long for the shoes left in the wrong place or the television turned up too loud.

There were days when she would have given anything to be annoyed by him one more time.

And I think that is one of the strangest parts of grief.

You can be surrounded by people who love you. You can laugh. You can go to dinner. You can have moments when life actually feels good again.

And still, underneath all of it, there can be this ache for one particular person.

Because there is no substitute for the person you are missing.

Sometimes you are simply homesick for someone you will never see again in this lifetime.

That is one of the reasons I wrote When Grief & Loss Won’t Shut Up.

I wanted to put words around the parts of grief that are so hard to explain. The missing. The longing. The strange moments when life looks completely normal from the outside while inside you are thinking, “I just want my person back.”

If you know this kind of homesickness, this book was written for you.

📖 Get your copy of When Grief & Loss Won’t Shut Up today and find words for some of the things you may have been carrying quietly on your own.

👉 Tap “Order Now” to get your copy today.

ad_creative_bodies:
💔 Grief really can feel like being sad every minute of every day.  Not necessarily crying every minute.

Not necessarily falling apart every minute.

But carrying a sadness that seems to sit underneath everything.

You can be driving to the store, answering an email, folding laundry, talking to someone, even laughing at something funny...

and the grief is still there.

There is this strange melancholy that follows you around.

Sometimes it is loud.

Sometimes it is barely noticeable.

Sometimes you are having what looks like a perfectly normal day and then, out of nowhere, you remember again.

They are gone.

And for a second, it can feel like you are learning it all over again.

That is one of the things people do not always understand about grief.

You can function and still be deeply sad.

You can smile and still miss them terribly.

You can have a good moment and still feel the ache underneath it.

You can keep living your life while also wishing with everything in you that one enormous part of it had never changed.

And sometimes that is exhausting.

Because there is no real “off” switch.

You do not clock out of grief at five o’clock.

You do not leave it in the car when you walk into the grocery store.

You do not put it away because everyone around you seems ready for things to feel normal again.

Grief comes with you.

That is one of the reasons I wrote When Grief & Loss Won’t Shut Up.

I wanted to talk about the parts of grief that can be so hard to explain to other people. The sadness that lingers. The thoughts that keep coming back. The strange experience of continuing to live your life while missing someone every single day.

If grief seems to be following you everywhere right now, this book was written for you.

📖 Get your copy of When Grief & Loss Won’t Shut Up today and let it help put words around some of what you have been carrying.

I was 73, and I thought nothing could surprise me anymore. But nothing in my long, complicated, beautiful life prepared me for the humiliation I felt that Sunday afternoon at my great-grandson's christening.
It was supposed to be a perfect day. And it was. For everyone else. Friends, family, laughter, warm hugs. I stood near the front with my heart full as my grandson walked up holding the baby.
"Mom," he said, smiling proudly. "Come say hi to little James."
Everyone turned toward me. Waiting. Expecting. Smiling. I opened my mouth to greet the baby and nothing came out. His name, a name I had heard a hundred times over the past month, was gone. Vanished.
I stared at his sweet little face and my mind went blank. Dead air. My throat tightened. My chest squeezed. Heat crawled up my cheeks. And as I looked around, I watched their expressions shift. Confusion. Concern. Then pity.
And pity cuts deeper than any insult. It wounds the soul. 💔
The whispers started. Not out loud but I felt them. "Poor woman… she's slipping." "That's what happens at her age."
I wanted to disappear. That moment cracked something inside me.
That night I couldn't sleep. I stared at the ceiling, tears sliding quietly down my face. My name is Ruth Calloway. I live in a small town just outside of Greenville, South Carolina. And I will never forget that night. The night I felt myself fading. Slowly becoming invisible to the people I loved. Losing my mind one forgotten moment at a time. 😢
The senior moments kept multiplying. I'd forget where I put my keys. Why I walked into a room. Full conversations I'd had hours earlier. The fog rolled in thick and heavy, making it impossible to think straight. Even reading became difficult. Holding onto a thought felt like trying to carry water in my hands. I was terrified.
But I hid it. Smiled through it. Pretended everything was fine. I didn't want anyone to worry. But my daughter Rebecca saw right through me. She never said anything directly, but her eyes did. That quiet fear. That silent sadness.
And the worst part? I saw doubt in my granddaughter's eyes too. Like she wasn't sure she could trust me alone with the baby. 😞
That shattered me.
Meanwhile the bills kept rising. Groceries, utilities, gas, medications. Everything cost more. My savings were dwindling. Social Security wasn't enough. I felt useless. Small. Afraid.
Until one day Rebecca said:
"Mom, the couple who owns the company I work for is looking for a part-time nanny. Just a few days a week. Their newborn son. They're very private, very kind, and I mentioned you."
"Me?" I blinked. "A nanny?"
"They want someone mature," she said softly. "Gentle. Trustworthy. Someone like you."
I wanted to say no. I was scared I'd forget something important. That I'd fail. But stronger than that fear was my need to feel needed again.
So I said yes.
A few days later I stood in front of a beautiful home just outside of town. Not flashy. But intentional. Warm wood everywhere. Books lining the hallways. A garden that someone clearly loved. The kind of place that felt lived in, not just decorated.
The woman who opened the door was tall, graceful, elegant without trying. But her eyes were soft.
"You must be Ruth," she said. "I'm Claudette. Please come in."
She was in her early sixties maybe. But there was something about her. Sharp. Present. Grounded. She showed me around, introduced me to baby Eli, walked me through every detail. Feeding times, nap routines, the lullaby playlist. Then just as I picked up my purse to leave she said something that stopped me.
"This job isn't just about the baby."
I frowned. "What do you mean?"
"It's about you too," she said calmly. "Most people think aging means decline. It doesn't. Not if you know what's really happening inside your brain."
I didn't know what to say. So I smiled politely and left. But her words stayed with me.
The next week I started. Nervous but hopeful. Claudette treated me not like an employee but like a welcomed guest. Every conversation felt intentional. Gentle. Awake.
One evening after Eli fell asleep I found her in the library. A fire glowed behind her. She sat in an armchair, eyes closed, wearing a pair of sleek headphones.
"Sorry," I whispered. "Didn't mean to interrupt."
She opened her eyes slowly, smiling.
"You didn't. I'm just tuning in. Would you like to try?"
"What is it?" I asked.
She paused for a moment. Then she said something I wasn't expecting.
"Ruth, do you know why some people stay sharp into their eighties and nineties while others fade? It's not luck. It's not genetics. There's something in your brain right now, a protein that researchers have been studying quietly for years. Harvard. The National Institute of Aging. They call it the memory protein. When it's active, your mind is clear, your memory works, your thinking is sharp."
I felt my hands go still in my lap. She kept going.
"But after a certain age, especially after stress and grief, it goes dormant. And nobody tells you. Because the people who profit from you staying foggy and medicated don't want you to know it can be reactivated."
She held out another pair of headphones.
"This is something that was developed years ago through research most people have never heard of. It sends a signal that wakes that protein back up. Ten seconds. That's all."
I looked at her. "Is this a joke?"
She smiled. "Just try it."
I almost didn't. It seemed too simple. Too quiet. Nothing about it looked like something that could help a woman who had just forgotten her great-grandson's name in front of her entire family.
But I had nothing left to lose.
I placed the headphones on. And I don't know how to explain what happened. I just know that everything got quiet. Not outside. Inside. The noise that had been running in my head for months, the worry, the fog, the constant reaching for things that weren't there anymore, it all went still.
That night I slept deeply. No tossing. No spiraling thoughts. Just peace.
The next morning I remembered something small. The name of my third-grade teacher. Then a recipe I hadn't made in decades. Then my neighbor's birthday, one I thought I had forgotten forever. At first it seemed random. Until it kept happening.
Day after day, something new came back online. 🙏
By the end of the week I called my sister and we talked for nearly an hour. I didn't lose my train of thought once. I didn't pause. I didn't fumble. My mind felt awake.
I kept listening every night. Ten seconds. That's all. It became my ritual. My reset.
My posture changed. My energy lifted. My confidence returned. I spoke clearer. Looked people in the eye again. I started sleeping through the night. Reading again, and actually remembering what I read.
My daughter said, "Mom… you haven't been this alive since I was a kid." 😭
And then one Sunday, a few months later, I was holding baby James at a family dinner. My grandson walked over and said, "He loves you, Mom. He always calms down when you hold him."
I looked down at that little face. And I remembered his name. His birthday. The story his father told me about picking it. Every detail. Clear as glass.
And I realized something in that moment. God doesn't close doors without opening others. Sometimes the opening is so quiet you almost miss it. But if you're paying attention, if you're brave enough to try something when you have no reason left to believe… the fog lifts. And you remember not just names and dates. You remember who you are.
Some things find you exactly when you need them. I believe this found me. 🙏
If you've felt the fog… if you've watched yourself fading… if you've seen pity in the eyes of people who used to look at you with respect…
Watch the video. You won't find it through a search. Things like this have a way of disappearing quietly, and I don't know how long it stays up.
But if it's still there when you tap below, don't wait. You've waited long enough.
👉 Tap below to see if it's still available.
It brought me back to my family. It brought me back to myself.
Maybe it'll bring you back too. God bless you. 🙏
